content: Agitation is characterized by excessive motor activity accompanied by an internal sense of tension. It can also be defined as inappropriate verbal, vocal, or motor activity that is not directly related to apparent needs. Key features of agitation include motor restlessness and an exaggerated response to external stimuli. In severe cases, agitation may escalate into aggression or even overt violent behavior. Aggression typically involves verbal abuse, physical or verbal threats, and threats of violence. Agitated or violent behavior accounts for approximately 10% of all emergency psychiatric interventions. Psychotic symptoms, such as delusions or hallucinations, are strongly associated with aggressive and violent behavior, with individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia being particularly prone to agitation. Over a lifetime, about 1% of the population will develop schizophrenia, and more than 90% of individuals with schizophrenia will experience agitation, averaging 11–12 episodes of acute agitation annually. Psychotic agitation is clinically significant due to the distress it causes patients and the risks it poses to both the patients themselves and others, including healthcare staff and other service users, particularly in emergency or inpatient psychiatric settings. Guidelines for managing psychosis-induced agitation and violence recommend both non-pharmacological and pharmacological interventions. In the UK, rapid tranquillization is defined as the use of psychotropic medication to control agitated, threatening, or destructive psychotic behavior. It is recommended in situations where rapid control of agitation, aggression, or excitement is necessary, and when less coercive techniques, such as verbal de-escalation, have failed. Pharmacological management of acute agitation has traditionally involved four classes of medications: barbiturates, benzodiazepines, and firstand second-generation antipsychotics. Loxapine, a first-generation antipsychotic, has traditionally been administered orally or intramuscularly. A Cochrane systematic review concluded that loxapine is a viable option for rapid tranquillization in acute psychosis. Other studies have also demonstrated its effectiveness in managing hostility and aggression in individuals with schizophrenia. More recently, loxapine has been tested in an inhaled form for the acute treatment of agitation in schizophrenia. The Staccato inhaler system delivers loxapine via a handheld, single-dose inhaler. This system rapidly heats pure loxapine to create an additive-free aerosol with particles small enough to penetrate deep into the lungs. This allows the medication to be delivered directly to the left side of the heart and into systemic circulation, resulting in a rapid onset of action comparable to intravenous administration. Inhaled loxapine has been shown to be effective at doses of 5 or 10 mg, with studies permitting up to three doses within a 24-hour period. The underlying cause of psychosis is thought to involve disturbances in neurotransmitter systems, particularly dopamine. Antipsychotics exert their anti-agitation effects primarily by inhibiting dopaminergic transmission, as well as through histamine and noradrenaline blockade, although the exact mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Loxapine blocks postsynaptic mesolimbic D1 and D2 dopamine receptors, as well as 5-HT2A serotonin receptors. It also blocks histaminic (H1), muscarinic (M), and adrenergic (α-1 and α-2) receptors. Although classified as a first-generation antipsychotic, loxapine shares structural similarities with the second-generation antipsychotic clozapine and has a serotonin-to-dopamine binding affinity ratio similar to that of second-generation antipsychotics. Inhaled loxapine exhibits pharmacokinetics and a rapid onset of action comparable to intravenous administration, making it a novel and effective treatment for acute agitation in schizophrenia. Managing agitation in psychiatric settings, particularly in psychosis, poses significant challenges for clinicians, who must address acute symptoms while simultaneously making an accurate diagnosis. The use of antipsychotics for rapid tranquillization is often limited by factors such as sedation, route of administration, speed of onset, and adverse effects. Excessive sedation can delay accurate diagnosis and complicate further treatment. The goal of rapid tranquillization is to reduce agitation or aggression without inducing sedation, allowing the patient to participate in further assessment or treatment. First-generation antipsychotics are associated with significant movement disorders, which has led to the preference for second-generation antipsychotics as first-line treatments. Both oral and parenteral administration of antipsychotics are recommended for rapid tranquillization, but severely agitated patients often cannot cooperate with oral formulations. Additionally, parenteral administration is perceived as coercive and abusive by 93% of patients. There remains an unmet need for a non-invasive, rapidly acting treatment that effectively calms patients without excessive sedation, addresses underlying psychiatric symptoms, and is safe and tolerable. Such a treatment could significantly reduce the clinical and economic burden of agitation in inpatient psychiatric settings. Inhaled loxapine represents a novel approach to rapid tranquillization and has the potential to improve the management of psychotic agitation and aggression. It is important to systematically review and evaluate the effectiveness of this intervention, as no systematic reviews on this treatment currently exist.
